title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
authors: Daan van Hamersveld, Ewoud Smeur, Iurii Kriachko
abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.

infographic.key_insight: A reinforcement-learning controller enabled autonomous fixed-wing interception of maneuvering targets in real flight.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could extend autonomous interception beyond the short-range, low-altitude limits of quadcopters, though deployment cost and reliability remain unquantified.
method: Mapped filtered monocular-vision observations directly to actuator commands with a neural network.
Trained the policy using proximal policy optimization in a custom Python environment.
Compared against two classical guidance controllers in simulation and tested the policy in real flight.
infographic.evidence_signal: The policy outperformed classical controllers under most simulated conditions and successfully intercepted maneuvering fixed-wing targets in flight; the abstract provides no trial counts or success rates.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness across lighting, weather, sensing failures, and broader flight conditions is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning

title: QD-PINN:A Physics-Informed Neural Network Approach to Bayesian Quickest Detection in High-Dimensional Diffusions
authors: Hang Ye, Yi Liu, Haipeng Xing
abstract: Quickest detection problems (QDPs) arise in a wide range of applications. However, the complementarity structure of the associated variational inequalities poses substantial challenges for traditional numerical methods, particularly in high-dimensional settings. We propose a PINN-based framework for estimating the optimal stopping boundary in QDPs with high-dimensional diffusion processes and spatial dependence, while overcoming the curse of dimensionality. Theoretically, we establish a novel equivalence between the free-boundary PDE and an infinite-dimensional stochastic optimization problem, rigorously justifying the use of finite-dimensional neural networks to approximate the true solution. Furthermore, we assess the robustness of the proposed framework by quantifying uncertainty in the learned stopping boundaries using deep ensembles and Monte Carlo dropout. The results show low variability across independent training runs and stochastic forward passes, indicating stable and consistent boundary estimates. We also compare our PINN results with reference numerical solutions where available and find close agreement.

infographic.key_insight: QD-PINN uses physics-informed neural networks to estimate optimal stopping boundaries for Bayesian quickest detection in high-dimensional, spatially dependent diffusions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support timely change detection in systems modeled by correlated diffusion processes, where traditional numerical methods become difficult to scale.
method: Formulate quickest detection through a free-boundary PDE.
Establish equivalence to an infinite-dimensional stochastic optimization problem to justify neural-network approximation.
Assess stopping-boundary uncertainty using deep ensembles and Monte Carlo dropout.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports close agreement with reference numerical solutions where available and low boundary variability across independent training runs and stochastic forward passes.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational scaling or accuracy across dimensions, so practical high-dimensional performance remains to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: QD-PINN:A Physics-Informed Neural Network Approach to Bayesian Quickest Detection in High-Dimensional Diffusions

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Co-Adaptive Hip Exoskeleton Control (MARL-Exo) for Metabolic Energy Reduction
authors: Yifei Yuan, Jakob Wolf, Ghaith Androwis, Xianlian Zhou
abstract: Objective: This study aims to determine whether a hip-exoskeleton policy trained in simulation, by co-adapting with a musculoskeletal human model under a metabolic-energy reward, reduces the metabolic cost of walking in new users without per-user tuning, and how mechanical-power shaping affects the learned assistance. Methods: We developed MARL-Exo, a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework in which a full-body human model (304 muscle actuators; randomized anatomy, gait, and speed) and a bilateral hip-exoskeleton policy are trained concurrently in two stages. The exoskeleton observes only delayed hip kinematics and its past commands; its reward includes muscle metabolic power from a physiologically based energetics model, alone (Metabolic) or with mechanical-power shaping (Metabolic + Power). The Metabolic policy was deployed and tested without retraining in eight healthy adults walking at 1.25 m/s, using indirect calorimetry. Results: In simulation, the Metabolic policy reduced modeled muscle metabolic power by 13.8% relative to no-device walking, versus 8.8% for Metabolic + Power. On hardware, MARL-Exo reduced net metabolic rate by 18.3 $\pm$ 6.6% relative to Passive in all eight participants. Relative to No-Exo, the mean reduction was 7.4 $\pm$ 10.0%; six participants more than offset the 13.1% device-wearing penalty, walking up to 24.2% below their No-Exo cost. Conclusion: A metabolically informed policy co-adapted in simulation transferred to users without per-user tuning and consistently reduced the metabolic cost of walking with the device, while explicit power shaping reduced the simulated benefit. Significance: Unlike per-user human-in-the-loop optimization, this approach yields a single population-level controller and allows assistance objectives to be screened in simulation before human testing.

infographic.key_insight: A hip-exoskeleton controller co-trained with a simulated human reduced walking metabolic cost in new users without per-user tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation-based co-adaptation can produce a population-level assistance controller and screen reward designs before hardware testing.
method: Co-trained a 304-muscle human model and bilateral hip-exoskeleton policy in two stages, randomizing anatomy, gait, and speed.
Controlled assistance using only delayed hip kinematics and past commands.
Compared metabolic-only rewards with metabolic plus mechanical-power shaping, then deployed the metabolic-only policy without retraining.
infographic.evidence_signal: In eight healthy adults walking at 1.25 m/s, net metabolic rate fell 18.3 ± 6.6% versus Passive and 7.4 ± 10.0% versus No-Exo; simulated reductions were 13.8% with metabolic-only rewards versus 8.8% with added power shaping.
infographic.watch_item: Testing covered only eight healthy adults at one speed, and only six achieved metabolic costs below their No-Exo baseline.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning of Co-Adaptive Hip Exoskeleton Control (MARL-Exo) for Metabolic Energy Reduction

title: Graph Representation Learning via Adaptive Expectile Aggregation
authors: Tianyi Zhu, Wei Lan
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) rely critically on neighborhood aggregation, yet conventional mean aggregation may fail to capture class-relevant distributional information, particularly in heterophilic graphs. We propose ExpectileGCN, an adaptive graph aggregation framework that introduces a learnable expectile level to capture neighborhood information beyond the mean. The proposed operator continuously adjusts aggregation between minimum- and maximum-type behaviors, with mean aggregation as a special case. A differentiable approximation based on sigmoid smoothing and fixed-point iterations enables end-to-end optimization. Theoretically, we establish stability properties and transductive generalization guarantees for ExpectileGCN. We further investigate its classification risk under heterophilic neighborhood models. For informative neighborhoods, we show that expectile aggregation can exploit class-dependent scale differences to achieve a classification advantage over mean aggregation. Under a local asymptotic regime with diminishing per-neighbor label informativeness, we establish that this advantage can persist in terms of limiting classification risk. Experiments on homophilic and heterophilic benchmark graphs demonstrate strong predictive performance and improved robustness under feature corruption and structural perturbations.

infographic.key_insight: ExpectileGCN learns how to aggregate graph neighborhoods beyond the mean, capturing class-relevant distributional differences, especially in heterophilic graphs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive aggregation may improve graph-based prediction and resilience to corrupted features or perturbed connections.
method: Learn an expectile level that shifts aggregation between minimum- and maximum-type behavior, with the mean as a special case.
Use sigmoid smoothing and fixed-point iterations for end-to-end differentiation.
Analyze stability, transductive generalization, and classification risk under heterophilic neighborhood models.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports strong predictive performance and improved robustness on homophilic and heterophilic benchmarks, but provides no dataset names or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Fixed-point iterations introduce computational and convergence considerations whose practical costs are not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Graph Representation Learning via Adaptive Expectile Aggregation

title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
authors: Tongkun Guan, Zhibo Yang, Mingkun Yang, Haocheng Wang, Wei Shen, Xiaokang Yang
abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: PerceptRL makes fine-grained visual perception rewardable by converting verified caption errors into labeled questions and supervising spatial fidelity during tool-assisted inspection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a post-training recipe for improving multimodal models’ visual accuracy and reducing error propagation from incorrect crops or annotations.
method: Extract and verify caption errors with a multi-agent pipeline, then build chain and multiple-choice QA with rule-based rewards.
Train through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL.
Use Coordinate Injection in cold-start trajectories and grounding-aware process rewards to improve spatial tool use.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, exceeding the base model with the same tools by 15.7 percentage points and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 5.2 points.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation depends on reliable error verification and spatial supervision; the abstract does not report their cost or robustness across new domains.
infographic.paper_title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions

title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time
authors: Elisabeth Fink
abstract: Self-attention mechanisms have established the Transformer as the dominant backbone across natural language processing, source code intelligence, and automated theorem proving. However, all-to-all pairwise token comparison enforces a quadratic $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ compute and memory barrier alongside severe softmax attention dilution as sequence length $N$ scales beyond the training horizon. Inspired by recent advances in algebraic graph learning (\textbf{WPNet}), this work introduces \textbf{GTFormer}, a syntax-free hierarchical Graph Neural Network (GNN) that replaces flat self-attention for general long-context sequence modeling. GTFormer organizes raw token streams into a bounded-degree hierarchy combining a balanced binary reduction tree ($\lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ depth), horizontal boundary-bridging shift edges, random expander shortcuts, multi-channel convex highway gating, and a top-down broadcast pass. Across eight long-context code, log, and multi-hop retrieval benchmarks trained exclusively on sequences of length $N \le 512$, GTFormer extrapolates zero-shot to $N = 4{,}194{,}304$ ($8192\times$) on a single commodity GPU in linear $\mathcal{O}(N)$ memory, maintaining near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers suffer from out-of-distribution attention collapse and out-of-memory exhaustion.

infographic.key_insight: GTFormer replaces self-attention with a syntax-free hierarchical graph, reporting near-perfect accuracy at sequence lengths 8192× beyond its maximum training length.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture could enable long-context code, log, and retrieval processing on a single commodity GPU with linear rather than quadratic memory scaling.
method: Build a balanced binary token hierarchy with logarithmic depth.
Add boundary-bridging shift edges and random expander shortcuts.
Combine multi-channel convex highway gating with top-down broadcasting.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight benchmarks, the abstract reports training only at N ≤ 512 and zero-shot evaluation up to 4,194,304 tokens, with near-perfect accuracy where standard and RoPE Transformers degrade or exhaust memory.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify benchmark details, GPU hardware, or runtime measurements, limiting assessment of generalization and practical linear-time performance.
infographic.paper_title: GTFormer: A Syntax-Free Graph Network Alternative to Transformers for 8192$\times$ Length Extrapolation in Linear Time

title: Agentic Distributional Regression: Conditional Density Estimation through Agent-Written Programs
authors: Lorenzo Tedesco
abstract: In this paper we propose a method for estimating conditional densities from an iid sample using a language-model agent. The agent writes the estimator as a short program that, for each covariate value, returns the estimated conditional distribution of the response. The program is built from a library of probability distributions, so the returned law can be a parametric distribution, a mixture or a multivariate factorization, with parameters given by explicit functions of the covariates. Since the number of operations and constants in the program is limited, the fitted conditional density is a formula that can be inspected and evaluated independently of the agent, while the choice of the model structure and of the fitting procedure is left to the agent. We call this approach agentic distributional regression (ADR). Treating the returned program as a random conditional density estimator, we derive a finite-sample error bound under explicit complexity and optimization assumptions, and an oracle inequality for selection using independent validation data. For a stably selected regular structure with sufficiently accurate fitting, we obtain asymptotic normality of the fitted constants. In simulation studies, on twelve real datasets and on a new dataset collected after the agents' training data, ADR with Claude Opus 5.5 has the best average performance among the methods considered.

infographic.key_insight: Agentic distributional regression uses a language-model agent to write compact, inspectable programs that estimate conditional probability distributions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The fitted estimator can be evaluated independently of the agent, providing a portable formula for predicting response distributions from input variables.
method: Construct distributions, mixtures or multivariate factorizations from a probability-distribution library.
Let the agent choose model structure and fitting procedure within limits on program operations and constants.
Analyze finite-sample error, independent-validation selection and asymptotic behavior under stated assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports the best average performance among tested methods for ADR with Claude Opus 5.5 across simulations, twelve real datasets and a new dataset collected after the agents’ training data.
infographic.watch_item: The theoretical guarantees depend on explicit complexity, optimization and regularity assumptions; compact code alone does not ensure accurate fitting.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Distributional Regression: Conditional Density Estimation through Agent-Written Programs

title: Interpretable Meta-Policies for Neural Decision Making
authors: Raban Emunds, Jannis Blüml, Quentin Delfosse, Kristian Kersting
abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning remains difficult to interpret and align due to the black-box nature of neural networks. While (neuro-)symbolic approaches improve transparency by incorporating symbolic reasoning, applying them directly to low-level actions results in overly complex, unreadable policies. We introduce NEXUS, a hierarchical RL framework that resolves this tension by combining neural skills with symbolic meta-policies. By shifting transparent reasoning to high-level skills rather than atomic actions, NEXUS drastically reduces symbolic complexity without sacrificing environment performance. Object-centric observations enable high-level reasoning and the design of reward functions and meta-policies by interaction with LLMs. We demonstrate that NEXUS agents learn disentangled skills, are interpretable regarding high-level goals, are better aligned to goals described in the game manual, less prone to reward hacking and more robust to game simplifications than deep RL. Finally, we isolate and evaluate the impact of different meta-policy architectures (neural, symbolic, neuro-symbolic) on environmental return and aligned task performance.

infographic.key_insight: NEXUS makes reinforcement learning more interpretable by using symbolic meta-policies to select high-level neural skills instead of low-level actions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Separating transparent goal selection from neural execution can help engineers inspect agent behavior and align it with intended tasks.
method: Combine neural skills with symbolic meta-policies in a hierarchical RL framework.
Use object-centric observations for high-level reasoning and LLM-assisted reward and meta-policy design.
Compare neural, symbolic, and neuro-symbolic meta-policy architectures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reduced symbolic complexity without sacrificing environment performance, improved task alignment, less reward hacking, and greater robustness to game simplifications than deep RL.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative results or benchmark details, leaving the magnitude and generality of the reported benefits unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Interpretable Meta-Policies for Neural Decision Making

title: Collective Dynamics of Self-Reinforcement: How Cross-Task Coupling Drives Policy Collapse in Unsupervised RLVR
authors: Peize Ding
abstract: Label-free reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) rewards a language model for agreeing with its own majority vote. It improves reasoning at first but eventually collapses: the self-assessed reward goes to one while accuracy falls, often until the model gives the same answer to every problem. The collapse appears only when training uses many problems. We explain this dataset-size dependence as a collective instability. In a solvable many-problem model in which problems share parameters, a population whose problems prefer different answers amplifies any shared perturbation for as long as the population-averaged slope $\langle F'\rangle$ of the single-problem self-reinforcement drift $F$ is positive. This holds while problems are still uncertain about their answers. Per-problem sharpening, slowed by $1/N$ for $N$ training problems, races against the shared mode, which grows at a rate $\proptoλ^2$ independent of $N$, where $λ$ is the strength of the shared coupling. This yields a critical number of problems $N_c\simeq\ln(1/δ)/(λ^2G)$, where $δ$ seeds the shared mode and $G$ decreases with the initial confidence. Simulations of the model confirm the predictions: a sharp transition, $N_c\proptoλ^{-2}$ up to a logarithmic correction, a single critical amplification $λ^2NG$ across couplings, confidence profiles and training variants, a logarithmic dependence on batch size, and no collapse for confident initial models. A kernel version of the theory identifies a protective coupling (generalization of sharpening) and a marginal-entropy bonus that stabilizes the uniform collective mode. In label-free RL of a small Transformer, removing the shared direction prevents collapse entirely, restoring it causes collapse, and collapse grows with training-set size and base-model entropy.

infographic.key_insight: Cross-task parameter sharing can turn majority-vote self-reinforcement into a collective instability, driving reward toward one while accuracy collapses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Scaling label-free RLVR to more training problems can increase collapse risk when shared amplification outpaces per-problem answer sharpening.
method: Derive a solvable many-problem model comparing shared-mode growth with per-problem sharpening.
Predict a critical dataset size governed by coupling strength, initial confidence, and perturbation size.
Test predictions in simulations and probe shared-direction effects in a small Transformer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations support a sharp collapse transition and approximately inverse-square coupling dependence; small-Transformer experiments prevent collapse by removing the shared direction and restore it by reinstating that direction.
infographic.watch_item: Validation uses a simplified model and a small Transformer; applicability to larger models and practical stabilization methods needs further testing.
infographic.paper_title: Collective Dynamics of Self-Reinforcement: How Cross-Task Coupling Drives Policy Collapse in Unsupervised RLVR

title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning
authors: Kheer Sagar Patel, Mojtaba Soltanalian
abstract: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.

infographic.key_insight: For structure-encoded tasks, more examples may narrow but need not eliminate the finite-resource gap between example-only learning and methods given the governing structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: When validated operators, physical laws, graphs, or constraints are available, encode them before training and reserve learning for unspecified components.
method: Define the structure gap in finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification.
Prove Gaussian inverse-problem excess risk, a cell-coverage lower bound, and unobserved-orbit non-identifiability.
Test the mechanisms in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports exact Gaussian risk results and controlled experiments, including graph-size extrapolation, but provides no numerical effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: The advantage depends on validated governing structure; the results do not establish universal superiority over data-driven learning.
infographic.paper_title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning

title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution
authors: Daniel Beránek
abstract: Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations. A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral. The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.

infographic.key_insight: Separate evidence used for agent reasoning from evidence authorized to justify persistent identity changes in entity resolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A commit-time authorization guardrail could limit unsupported identity-changing graph mutations without restricting exploratory agent reasoning.
method: Map selected DIO/ODI reconstruction-failure distinctions to domain-governed, identity-preserving constraints.
Promote evidence separately for each claim; UNVERIFIED admission grants no authorization eligibility.
Use a two-phase supervisor to check proposition coverage, conflict resolution, authorized scope, and state/policy version validity before commit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper proposes evaluation against generic authorization and conventional identifier rules but reports no implementation or empirical validation.
infographic.watch_item: Protection depends on adequate domain policies, evidence promotion, and enforcement; hypothesis-conditioned retrieval remains unaddressed.
infographic.paper_title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution

title: An Input Skip Can Reparameterize a VAE Without Improving the Generator
authors: Kevin Lee
abstract: An input skip can reduce reconstruction error while leaving a model's distribution of new samples unchanged. For a Gaussian variational autoencoder (VAE) with constant input skip $0\leqα<1$, a model without a skip can be written in skip form by multiplying its decoder output by $b=1-α$ and its noise variance by $b^2$. The distribution of observations and latent variables and its exact generative scores stay the same, while reconstruction mean squared error (MSE) is multiplied by $b^2$. Separate training can produce different generators because optimization depends on the parameter coordinates. In a Gaussian experiment with known density, changing skip and observation variance together reduces MSE but worsens energy score and the estimate of negative log density from importance sampling. On seven annual Deep-ocean Assessment and Reporting of Tsunamis (DART) records, energy score differences at the same observation variance have both signs on four original records and favor the skip on three records from 2018. Probabilistic principal component analysis (PPCA) has lower mean energy scores than every neural DART fit. With the encoder and decoder kept the same, estimating observation variance from training reconstruction error can also worsen energy score. Assessing generation requires more than reconstruction error.

infographic.key_insight: An input skip can lower VAE reconstruction error without changing the generated distribution, so better reconstruction does not necessarily mean better generation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate generative quality separately from reconstruction MSE, especially when changing skip strength or observation variance.
method: Derive a Gaussian VAE reparameterization for constant input skip α, with b = 1 − α.
Scale decoder output by b and noise variance by b², preserving the joint distribution while scaling reconstruction MSE by b².
Evaluate separately trained models using energy score and, on known-density Gaussian data, importance-sampled negative log density.
infographic.evidence_signal: Gaussian experiments showed lower MSE alongside worse generative scores; seven annual DART records showed mixed skip benefits, while PPCA achieved lower mean energy scores than every neural DART fit.
infographic.watch_item: The exact equivalence applies to the specified Gaussian reparameterization; separate training can change generators, and reconstruction-based variance estimation can worsen energy score.
infographic.paper_title: An Input Skip Can Reparameterize a VAE Without Improving the Generator

title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
authors: Saket Reddy, Amro Abbas, Anshuman Suri, Ari Morcos, David Schwab, Pratyush Maini
abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

infographic.key_insight: Benign-looking instruction data can erode LLM safety, and gradient alignment can help identify which training examples contribute to unsafe behavior.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SimpleLoRIF makes gradient-based safety filtering practical for million-example post-training datasets while largely preserving model capability.
method: Simplify low-rank gradient attribution and restrict backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks.
Rank fine-tuning examples by gradient alignment with unsafe responses.
Create SafeTulu by removing the 20% of Tulu 3 examples most aligned with unsafe responses.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports emergent-misalignment detection AUC up to 0.865 and GCG attack success rate reductions up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering.
infographic.watch_item: Reported gains do not establish universal safety; filtering effectiveness may depend on the unsafe-response probes, model, and evaluation attacks.
infographic.paper_title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data

title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents
authors: Milad Sikaroudi
abstract: Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.

infographic.key_insight: Concordat makes action rules runtime-enforced finite-state protocols rather than relying on an LLM agent to obey prompt instructions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its Python interface helps protect consequential workflows by blocking illegal tool calls before side effects and reserving human decisions for humans.
method: Expose only tools permitted in the current protocol state and reject out-of-protocol calls.
Check protocols at definition time and reject subclasses that could bypass inherited constraints.
Charge and split token and tool-call budgets linearly across agent handoffs.
infographic.evidence_signal: On tau-bench’s 50 airline tasks with simulated customer pressure, Concordat had zero confirmation violations versus 13/50 GPT-4.1 tasks and 29/128 Claude Haiku 5.5 task-runs for the standard agent, with no significant task-success difference.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the reported airline benchmark; deployment still requires correctly specified protocols covering consequential actions.
infographic.paper_title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents

title: Bayes-Adaptive MDPs for Rollout Allocation to Enhance GRPO Training
authors: Faeze Moradi Kalarde, Armin Toroghi, Nam Ho Koh, Doo Hwan Hwang, Seungjin Kim, Kee-Eung Kim
abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has demonstrated strong performance in LLM post-training. However, it allocates a uniform rollout budget to every training question, ignoring variations in question difficulty. As a result, highly difficult questions may receive too few rollouts to generate informative positive reward signals, limiting their contribution to training, while moderately difficult questions often receive more rollouts than necessary. In this work, we formulate the problem of difficulty-aware rollout budget allocation to maximize training utility under the same total rollout budget as standard GRPO. We propose AdaRoll-GRPO, which reformulates rollout allocation as a sequential decision-making problem and leverages a Bayes-adaptive Markov decision process (MDP) to learn an adaptive allocation policy. The learned policy is computed offline and applied during GRPO training without introducing additional online optimization overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning datasets and LLM architectures demonstrate that AdaRoll-GRPO consistently improves GRPO training performance under a fixed rollout budget, highlighting the effectiveness of adaptive rollout allocation for GRPO in LLM post-training.

infographic.key_insight: AdaRoll-GRPO adaptively allocates rollouts across training questions to improve GRPO performance under the same total rollout budget.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Difficulty-aware rollout allocation can make LLM post-training more effective without adding online allocation-policy optimization.
method: Formulate rollout allocation as sequential decision-making under a fixed total budget.
Use a Bayes-adaptive MDP to compute an adaptive allocation policy offline.
Apply the learned policy during GRPO training instead of allocating uniformly.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent improvements over GRPO across multiple reasoning datasets and LLM architectures at a fixed rollout budget, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Offline policy computation adds setup work, and transfer to new models or question distributions should be validated.
infographic.paper_title: Bayes-Adaptive MDPs for Rollout Allocation to Enhance GRPO Training

title: An end-to-end framework for uncertainty-aware validation of generative models
authors: Giada Badaracco, Sean Benevedes, Christina Reissel, Philip Harris, Gaia Grosso
abstract: Density estimation with generative models is a common task in the physical sciences, for example in background estimation in particle physics. Existing machine learning techniques, however, lack methods to quantify uncertainties that can be propagated into a statistical test. That limits the validation of generative models to standard goodness-of-fit tests, in which the generative model is treated as exact (point-null hypothesis). But a model fitted to a finite training set is never exact, so if its uncertainties are neglected, any sufficiently powerful goodness-of-fit test will eventually reject it once the test set is large enough to resolve this estimation error. We propose SIGMA, an end-to-end framework combining density estimation with principled uncertainty quantification. We use Gaussian mixture models, for which uncertainties are tractable, and further construct a new goodness-of-fit test in which these uncertainties are profiled as nuisance parameters to account for the statistical error of the fit, promoting the conventional point-null test to a composite one. A rejection then signals genuine mismodeling rather than a test set large enough to resolve the error of the fit, provided the propagated uncertainties faithfully cover that error. We demonstrate the framework on a controlled two-dimensional toy model and on a collider physics benchmark modeling the QCD background process. With uncertainties included, the same model can be trusted on test sets up to an order of magnitude larger than the standard test allows. Our work thus provides a statistically grounded basis for a robust use of generative models in the physical sciences.

infographic.key_insight: SIGMA propagates generative-model fitting uncertainty into validation, helping distinguish genuine mismodeling from finite-training-set error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Uncertainty-aware validation can support more reliable use of learned background models in particle physics and other physical sciences.
method: Estimate densities with Gaussian mixture models whose fitting uncertainties are tractable.
Profile these uncertainties as nuisance parameters in a new goodness-of-fit test.
Replace an exact-model point null with a composite null that accounts for statistical fitting error.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a controlled 2D toy model and a collider QCD-background benchmark, including uncertainties allowed the same model to be trusted on test sets up to an order of magnitude larger than standard testing allowed.
infographic.watch_item: The interpretation of rejection depends on propagated uncertainties faithfully covering fitting error; the framework uses Gaussian mixture models rather than arbitrary generators.
infographic.paper_title: An end-to-end framework for uncertainty-aware validation of generative models

title: Uncovering Why LLMs Fail: From Internal Mechanisms to Adversarial Reasoning Trajectories
authors: Zirui Ding, Xinxin Fan, Hao Yuan, Shaoye Luo, Men Niu, Yunfeng Lu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are usually evaluated by final-output correctness or safety, yet an endpoint label does not reveal how a failure develops throughout the reasoning process. We therefore ask whether ordinary reasoning failures and adversarially induced failures can be characterized using the same internal coordinates. Towards this end, we in this paper study a white-box diagnostic framework CauTrace to disclose the root-cause of why LLM fails from three fundamental inspections: Functional States, Propagation of Representation, Temporal-State Coordination and Reasoning Trajectory. First, seven functional states are creatively defined to represent the support and constraint processing in LLMs. Second, the propagation of representation change measures how the changes among the seven states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks. Third, temporal-state coordination and trajectory topology characterize when the commitment and verification occur relative to the support, and how the dominant state sequence evolves over the full inference process. Finally, we evaluate CauTrace on both clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. Across Qwen and LLaMA-family models, the failed traces show weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, while the exact representation-level signatures and timing shifts vary by architecture. Held-out repair and steering tests demonstrate consistent operational signals that were in line with our claims for certain models and specific settings, with aligned steering producing the predicted directional changes in process measures. Overall, CauTrace provides a unified diagnostic framework for analyzing failure dynamics through changes in support, commitment, and verification, which would shed light on the in-depth research on LLM security.

infographic.key_insight: CauTrace diagnoses ordinary and adversarial LLM failures through shared internal measures of support, commitment, verification, and reasoning trajectories.
infographic.engineering_relevance: White-box process diagnostics can complement output-level testing by identifying internal failure patterns that may inform targeted repair and steering.
method: Define seven functional states for support and constraint processing.
Measure how state-related representation changes persist across Transformer blocks.
Track support, commitment, and verification timing alongside dominant-state trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Qwen and LLaMA-family evaluations of clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations, failed traces showed weaker Attention–MLP agreement on support updates and less verification relative to commitment.
infographic.watch_item: Signatures and timing vary by architecture, while repair and steering evidence is limited to specific models and settings; implementation also requires internal model access.
infographic.paper_title: Uncovering Why LLMs Fail: From Internal Mechanisms to Adversarial Reasoning Trajectories

title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
authors: Zhen Yang, Wen Wang, Xander Xu, Ying-Cong Chen
abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

infographic.key_insight: In simulated worlds with altered physics, LLMs struggled to independently notice anomalies and discover the hidden laws without research prompts or hints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Autonomous scientific agents need stronger anomaly detection and experiment design to investigate unexpected behavior without predefined objectives.
method: LongChang generates simulated scenes with one or more altered physical laws.
Explorer LLMs manipulate objects and build tools to investigate self-chosen questions.
Separate agents review scenes, tools, and reports, using exploration records to guide scene evolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 12 evaluated LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieved a 16.7% discovery rate and the other 11 scored 0%; exploration records showed missed anomalies and partial law identification.
infographic.watch_item: Results rely on simulated physics and LLM-based evaluation, so they do not establish performance in real-world scientific discovery.
infographic.paper_title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?

title: Clearing the FoG: Training KG Agents to Retrieve the Evidence Behind Their Answers
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Yingjun Du, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Haoran Luo
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer many factual questions correctly, but a correct answer is not necessarily a supported one. For an LLM agent, a knowledge graph (KG) plays two roles: as a source of answers, it supplies facts that the model lacks; as a source of evidence, it supplies the supporting triples that make an answer traceable and auditable. However, existing KG agents treat the KG only as a source of answers: their training data carries answers but not evidence, and their training rewards check the answer but not the retrieved evidence, so agents often answer correctly without retrieving the supporting triples. We propose FoG, a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. FoG consists of evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR): the synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions, so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction; the agent records the triples returned by the KG; and ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG enables 3B--4B open-source agents to outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.

infographic.key_insight: FoG trains knowledge-graph agents to retrieve supporting triples, making factual answers traceable rather than merely correct.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evidence-aware training can help engineers build auditable question-answering systems backed by retrieved knowledge-graph facts.
method: Synthesize evidence-grounded questions by recursively replacing explicit entities with verifiable sub-questions.
Record the triples returned during the agent’s knowledge-graph interactions.
Reward each supporting triple at the turn when the agent first retrieves it.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three KGQA benchmarks, the abstract reports that 3B–4B open-source agents outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires reliable supporting-triple annotations and retrieval logs; the abstract does not quantify their construction cost or robustness to incomplete graphs.
infographic.paper_title: Clearing the FoG: Training KG Agents to Retrieve the Evidence Behind Their Answers

title: Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis
authors: Andrew Szot, Samira Abnar, Omar Attia, Abbas Kazerouni, Michael Kirchhof, Cheng-Yu Hsieh
abstract: We explore how to build performant large language model (LLM) tool-use agents that complete complex, multi-step tasks. Specifically, we study how data composition in synthetically generated tool-use environments affects the training of such agents. To do so, we propose the SynthAPI pipeline, which explicitly controls the diversity of generated environments along the axes of tools, tasks, and the databases on which the tools operate. By systematically varying SynthAPI's generation controls in 458,752 tasks across 849 trained models of four different sizes, we derive a scaling law that predicts downstream tool-use agent generalization based on the scale and composition of the synthesized environments. These predictable relationships reveal several lessons for scaling tool-use agent data. As data budgets grow, scaling tool and database diversity becomes more effective than increasing the number of tasks, and increasing data complexity yields larger gains. Scaling according to these findings yields agents that outperform models trained on data from prior work in large-scale tool-use agent and synthetic environment generation across four evaluation benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: As synthetic training budgets grow, increasing tool and database diversity improves tool-use agent generalization more effectively than adding more tasks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent training pipelines should control environment composition, prioritizing broader tools, databases, and task complexity when scaling synthetic data.
method: Use SynthAPI to independently control tool, task, and database diversity.
Systematically vary synthetic environment composition across model sizes.
Fit a scaling law to predict downstream generalization from environment scale and composition.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study covers 458,752 tasks and 849 trained models across four model sizes; agents scaled using its findings outperform models trained on prior-work data across four evaluation benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether the scaling law transfers to production tools, unseen domains, or model sizes beyond those studied.
infographic.paper_title: Scaling Laws for Tool-Use Agents via Controllable Environment Synthesis
